name: IoT & Embedded Security
description: Security of IoT devices, embedded systems, firmware, and smart-home ecosystems.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers here (all USENIX 2018) map out the IoT security problem from several angles at once. Some take an offensive, systems-level view: BlackIoT: IoT Botnet of High Wattage Devices Can Disrupt the Power Grid (2018) showed that a botnet of heaters and air conditioners could be used to destabilize the bulk power grid, turning consumer IoT into a critical-infrastructure threat. Others looked at the software and platform layer, like Sensitive Information Tracking in Commodity IoT (2018), which applied taint tracking to smart-home apps, and at human factors, with Rethinking Access Control and Authentication for the Home Internet of Things (2018) recognizing that homes are multi-user, multi-relationship environments that classic access control ignores. A third strand attacked the devices themselves, from voice assistants in Skill Squatting Attacks on Amazon Alexa (2018) to sensor spoofing in Injected and Delivered (2018), while ACES (2018) and Inception (2018) began hardening and testing bare-metal embedded firmware directly.

A clear breakthrough across 2019-2020 was firmware analysis at scale. Because IoT firmware is hard to run outside its hardware, researchers built emulation and "re-hosting" techniques so firmware could be fuzzed automatically: FIRM-AFL (2019) introduced high-throughput greybox fuzzing via augmented process emulation, HALucinator (2020) re-hosted firmware by emulating its hardware abstraction layer, and Jetset (2021) and Fuzzware (2022) pushed targeted rehosting and precise MMIO modeling further. In parallel, the physical-sensor attack line matured from spoofing into striking demonstrations like Light Commands (2020), which injected voice commands into microphones using lasers, and defenses like SAVIOR (2020), which protected autonomous vehicles with physical invariants. Verified and cryptographic foundations also appeared, including VRASED (2019) for remote attestation and JEDI (2019) for end-to-end IoT encryption.

Alongside the device and firmware work, a large measurement and ecosystem-security thread grew up. All Things Considered (2019) gave the first large-scale empirical look at IoT devices in real homes, Looking from the Mirror (2019) probed device security through companion mobile apps, and Shattered Chain of Trust (2020) exposed flaws in cross-cloud access delegation. Voice assistants kept attracting scrutiny in SkillExplorer (2020), and The Circle Of Life (2021) characterized the full IoT malware lifecycle in the wake of Mirai.

Where the area stands now (2021-2022 here) is more holistic and deployment-aware. Firmware fuzzing has become precise and practical (Fuzzware, 2022), and bug-finding has scaled across many devices by exploiting shared input patterns in Sharing More and Checking Less (2021). Defense has shifted toward whole-system semantics: HAWatcher (2021) does semantics-aware anomaly detection across automated smart-home apps rather than per-device checks. And the agenda has broadened to the user's physical environment and privacy, with Lumos (2022) helping people find hidden IoT snooping devices in unfamiliar rooms. The arc runs from "IoT is insecure and even dangerous" toward scalable firmware analysis, verified building blocks, and context-aware, user-centric defenses.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this area, all clustered at NDSS 2018, wrestled with a basic problem: how do you even find bugs in devices you can barely instrument? IoTFuzzer (NDSS 2018) answered by fuzzing the companion smartphone app instead of the firmware itself, reaching deep into devices without source code, while "What You Corrupt Is Not What You Crash" (NDSS 2018) exposed why this is so hard, since memory corruption on embedded targets often causes no visible crash to detect. Alongside these bug-hunting efforts, a parallel track worried about the platform level rather than the device: "Fear and Logging in the Internet of Things" (NDSS 2018) and Decentralized Action Integrity (NDSS 2018) treated trigger-action and smart-home automation as the real attack surface.

That platform-and-safety thread grew into a dominant theme. IoTGuard (NDSS 2019) enforced security and safety policies dynamically across interacting rules, and IoTSafe (NDSS 2021) pushed further by discovering the physical interactions between devices that software analysis alone cannot see. In parallel, researchers realized that even perfectly secure software leaks information: Packet-Level Signatures (NDSS 2020) showed that encrypted smart-home traffic still betrays device activity, a privacy-inference concern that PFirewall (NDSS 2021) tried to mitigate. The hardware and systems community meanwhile built defensive primitives for constrained devices, from TIMBER-V's RISC-V enclaves (NDSS 2019) to return-address integrity in µRAI (NDSS 2020) and DMA compartmentalization in D-Box (NDSS 2022).

A striking mid-period shift was the rise of physical and analog attacks that bypass software entirely. SurfingAttack (NDSS 2020) injected inaudible ultrasonic commands into voice assistants, EarArray (NDSS 2021) defended against such attacks, and by 2023 the sensory attack surface had matured into a discipline of its own: Paralyzing Drones via EMI (NDSS 2023) and Un-Rocking Drones (NDSS 2023) laid out the foundations of acoustic and electromagnetic injection against MEMS sensors, the latter notably studying recovery, not just disruption. EM Eye (NDSS 2024) extended this to eavesdropping on embedded cameras through electromagnetic emissions.

The most recent work shows the field simultaneously scaling up and reaching into new domains. Firmware analysis grew more automated and large-scale, from "Faster and Better" (NDSS 2024) optimizing reaching-definition analysis on Linux-based firmware to a 2026 wave that fuses AI with classic techniques, most clearly FirmAgent (NDSS 2026), which pairs LLM agents with fuzzing for firmware vulnerability discovery, and FirmCross (NDSS 2026) tackling hybrid C-Lua web services. At the same time the target list keeps widening: IsolatOS and RTCON (both NDSS 2026) harden RTOS kernels, PhantomMotion (NDSS 2026) spoofs surveillance systems with lasers, HoneySat (NDSS 2026) builds satellite honeypots, and WiFinger (NDSS 2026) revisits the traffic-fingerprinting question that Packet-Level Signatures opened eight years earlier, now against noisier real-world data. The area has moved from finding memory bugs in a handful of home gadgets to securing a sprawling ecosystem of firmware, sensors, RTOS kernels, and even satellites, increasingly with AI in the loop.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work on this list treats IoT and embedded security as a foundations problem: understanding the threat and establishing trust before devices ever talk to each other. "Understanding Linux Malware" (S&P 2018) mapped the largely-ignored world of malware targeting the Linux-based systems that run most routers and IoT gadgets, while "Do You Feel What I Hear? Enabling Autonomous IoT Device Pairing Using Different Sensor Types" (S&P 2018) and "Secure Device Bootstrapping Without Secrets Resistant to Signal Manipulation Attacks" (S&P 2018) tackled the hard first step of getting devices to authenticate one another without human involvement or pre-shared secrets. By 2019 the community stepped back to take stock: "SoK: Security Evaluation of Home-Based IoT Deployments" (S&P 2019) became a heavily-cited anchor, documenting just how bleak the security practices of consumer smart-home devices really were and framing the agenda for years that followed.

Two big technical threads then took off. One is automated firmware analysis, driven by the reality that most embedded code is closed, hard to run off-device, and full of memory bugs. "Karonte: Detecting Insecure Multi-binary Interactions in Embedded Firmware" (S&P 2020) showed how to reason across the multiple cooperating binaries in a router image, and "DICE: Automatic Emulation of DMA Input Channels for Dynamic Firmware Analysis" (S&P 2021) attacked the rehosting problem of feeding realistic peripheral input to firmware under test. This line matured into a wave of fuzzers and analyses — "Diane" (S&P 2021), "HEAPSTER" on monolithic-firmware allocators (S&P 2022), and integrity/isolation defenses like "OAT: Attesting Operation Integrity of Embedded Devices" (S&P 2020) and "EC: Embedded Systems Compartmentalization via Intra-Kernel Isolation" (S&P 2023). The second thread is physical and analog attacks on the sensors and signals embedded systems depend on, systematized by "SoK: A Minimalist Approach to Formalizing Analog Sensor Security" (S&P 2020) and pushed forward by "Detection of Electromagnetic Interference Attacks on Sensor Systems" (S&P 2020), "Invisible Finger" against touchscreens (S&P 2022), "Inducing Wireless Chargers to Voice Out for Inaudible Command Attacks" (S&P 2023), and the measurement study "A Systematic Study of Physical Sensor Attack Hardness" (S&P 2024).

Alongside the systems work runs a distinctly human-centered strand: if devices are insecure by default, maybe markets and users can be nudged. "Ask the Experts: What Should Be on an IoT Privacy and Security Label?" (S&P 2020) and "Security Update Labels: Establishing Economic Incentives for Security Patching of IoT Consumer Products" (S&P 2020) argued for consumer-facing labels and patching incentives, followed by studies of what attributes actually move buyers (S&P 2021) and how real users reason about risk, from Reddit smart-home discussions (S&P 2023) to Chinese product teams' privacy practices (S&P 2026). Smart-home logic itself became an attack surface too, through work on messaging-protocol abuse ("Burglars' IoT Paradise", S&P 2020), trigger-action privacy (S&P 2021), and timing-based "Delay Wreaks Havoc on Your Smart Home" automation-interference attacks (S&P 2022).

The most recent work shows the field broadening in scope and adopting new tooling. Large language models have entered firmware testing directly with "LLMIF: Augmented Large Language Model for Fuzzing IoT Devices" (S&P 2024), complemented by response-guided "Labrador" (S&P 2024) and TEE-focused "SyzTrust" (S&P 2024). The 2026 cohort pushes into targets and process problems that earlier work left aside: "SoK: All You Ever Wanted to Know About Bootloader Security" (S&P 2026) systematizes the trust root every device starts from, "SatBleed" (S&P 2026) extends embedded security to commoditized satellite modules, "Fuzzing the Physical Space" (S&P 2026) brings physics-aware testing to industrial control systems, "Camveil" (S&P 2026) and "Bridge" (S&P 2026) keep advancing coordinated fuzzing and firmware taint analysis, and "Responsible Disclosure is a Two-Way Street" (S&P 2026) turns the lens on the broken vendor-researcher disclosure process itself — a sign the area now worries as much about ecosystem and lifecycle as about individual bugs.

ccs.narrative:
IoT and embedded security at CCS has addressed device firmware, smart-home automation, and safety of physical-world cyber-physical systems. The 2018 class revealed systemic risks in smart-home ecosystems: On the Safety of IoT Device Physical Interaction Control (CCS 2018) showed that physical interaction chains between IoT devices create safety hazards, If This Then What?: Controlling Flows in IoT Apps (CCS 2018) exposed information-flow violations in trigger-action platforms, and HoMonit: Monitoring Smart Home Apps from Encrypted Traffic (CCS 2018) demonstrated that misbehaving apps leave detectable network patterns even under encryption. Scission (CCS 2018) brought CAN-bus intrusion detection to automotive ECUs.

In 2019-2020, the focus shifted to firmware analysis. Charting the Attack Surface of Trigger-Action IoT Platforms (CCS 2019) systematically enumerated automation-rule attack vectors, Automatic Fingerprinting of Vulnerable BLE IoT Devices (CCS 2019) identified IoT devices at risk through their companion apps, and Examining Mirai's Battle over the Internet of Things (CCS 2020) measured the Mirai botnet's ongoing competition for vulnerable devices.

Black-box firmware fuzzing matured significantly: Snipuzz: Black-box Fuzzing of IoT Firmware via Message Snippet Inference (CCS 2021) fuzzed firmware without source code or emulation by inferring message structure from device responses. HoneyPLC: A Next-Generation Honeypot for Industrial Control Systems (CCS 2020) extended honeynet techniques to ICS/SCADA, capturing attacks including malicious ladder logic.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list, clustered around 2018, split along two lines that still define the field. One line treated the IoT device as an untrusted black box in someone's home: papers like Sensitive Information Tracking in Commodity IoT (USENIX 2018) and Fear and Logging in the Internet of Things (NDSS 2018) built taint-tracking and provenance logging for smart-home apps, while Rethinking Access Control and Authentication for the Home Internet of Things (USENIX 2018) argued that multi-user homes broke the single-owner security model. The other line went after the firmware and hardware itself: IoTFuzzer (NDSS 2018) fuzzed devices through their companion apps to find memory corruptions without firmware access, What You Corrupt Is Not What You Crash (NDSS 2018) exposed how hard crash detection is on embedded targets, and ACES (USENIX 2018) brought compartmentalization to bare-metal microcontrollers. Alongside these, BlackIoT (USENIX 2018) reframed the threat entirely, showing a botnet of high-wattage devices could destabilize the power grid.

By 2019-2020 the field matured in two directions. Systematization arrived with SoK: Security Evaluation of Home-Based IoT Deployments (S&P 2019), which gave the community a shared map of the attack surface, echoed by measurement work like All Things Considered (USENIX 2019) and the study of the Hajime botnet (NDSS 2019). At the same time, firmware analysis got dramatically more capable: FIRM-AFL (USENIX 2019) made greybox fuzzing of full firmware images practical through augmented process emulation, HALucinator (USENIX 2020) re-hosted firmware by emulating hardware abstraction layers, and Karonte (S&P 2020) tackled the multi-binary interactions inside embedded firmware that single-binary tools missed. Physical-layer and sensor attacks also came into focus, most memorably with Light Commands (USENIX 2020), which injected voice commands into smart speakers using lasers.

The 2021-2022 work pushed fuzzing toward the hardest cases. Snipuzz (CCS 2021) inferred message structure to fuzz IoT firmware as a black box over the network, and Fuzzware (USENIX 2022) used precise MMIO modeling to fuzz firmware without needing hardware in the loop, sharpening the re-hosting agenda that HALucinator had opened.

The most recent papers, from NDSS 2026, show the field both broadening and turning to new tools. Firmware bug-finding is being fused with machine intelligence in FirmAgent (NDSS 2026), which pairs LLM agents with fuzzing for vulnerability discovery, while RTOS internals get dedicated attention in IsolatOS (NDSS 2026) for double-fetch bugs and RTCON (NDSS 2026) for kernel fuzzing. The perennial themes recur in new settings: traffic-analysis fingerprinting continues in WiFinger (NDSS 2026), sensor-injection attacks extend to surveillance cameras in PhantomMotion (NDSS 2026), and the attack surface stretches to satellites (HoneySat) and extended-reality devices (From Perception to Protection). Together they signal a field that has moved from proving IoT is insecure to systematically hardening firmware, sensors, and the ever-widening edge.
